children: By Siyi Liu and Florence Tan

Oil traders in top consuming region Asia expect prices to remain elevated as fresh attacks dampen expectations for an imminent end to the Middle East conflict, while strong refining margins drive demand for physical supply.

Benchmark Brent crude futures climbed back above $100 a barrel last week and rose a further 3% on Monday to their highest since May, after Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia hit a key oil pipeline and Iran launched attacks on shipping.

The rally has spilled into physical markets, where spot premiums for benchmark Dubai and Oman crude rose last week to their highest since March, underscoring fierce competition for cargoes. Premiums for crude from West Africa, the U.S. and Latin America also hit multi-month highs.

"Unlike in March, when there was no oil, there is oil now but we have to pay much higher prices," said a trader with an Asian refiner, declining to be named as they were not authorised to speak to media.
PREMIUMS WELL ABOVE LAST MONTH'S LEVEL, TRADERS SAY
South Korea's SK Energy bought 4 million barrels of U.S. WTI crude for December arrival last week at premiums of about $24 a barrel to November ICE Brent swaps, trade sources said.
GS Caltex purchased 2 million barrels of U.S. crude at a similar premium to the November Dubai benchmark on delivered basis, the sources added.
That compares with a premium of about $13 a barrel to Dubai quotes on delivered basis for U.S. cargoes sold last month.

Chinese independent refiners, squeezed by dwindling Iranian and Russian supplies, have been scouring for alternatives. Shenchi Petrochemical last week bought al-Shaheen at about $23 a barrel above Dubai quotes on delivered basis, trade sources said.

"(The) crude market looks relatively constructive and it looks to be tightening," Andreas H. Lien, vice president of products trading at Equinor, said on the sidelines of last week's APPEC industry gathering.
"That is clearly because Asia starts pulling cargoes from the U.S. and South America again with a high delivered price point."
TIGHTENING SUPPLY, HORMUZ UNCERTAINTY
Three Asian refiners said they were running at full capacity to capture strong margins on products and petrochemicals.

Iraq's Basrah Medium remained widely available, but at premiums of about $20 a barrel to Dubai quotes for loading via ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, one of them said, compared with single-digit premiums last month.

Another three traders last week estimated 6 million to 8 million barrels a day of oil was passing through the Strait of Hormuz, while a naphtha trader estimated naphtha flows had recovered to 50-60% of pre-war levels.
Before the start of the Iran war on February 28, some 20% of the world's crude and liquefied natural gas supply transited the Strait of Hormuz.
Uncertainty over the pace of recovery in Hormuz flows has led to a wide range of price forecasts.

S&P Global Energy expects crude prices to average just under $100 per barrel next year under its base-case scenario. Prices could rise to $120 per barrel if disruptions to Hormuz traffic persist, but fall below $60 in a rapid-recovery scenario.

Wood Mackenzie forecast dated Brent prices to rise to near $110 per barrel around end-2026 and early 2027, before declining to around $60 per barrel until the beginning of 2028 on the assumption that flows via the Strait of Hormuz fully resume in January 2027.
